The project was started by the simple idea of “How much can I
overengineer plagiarism detection?”, an open ended task given to my
class by the professor of the Python scripting course. The solution can be
as simple as comparing different tree similarity metrics, finding optimal
metric weights for best accuracy, and submitting that as results.
Or we apply a more complex machine learning approach, using a graph
convolution network to learn the similarity of the source code’s abstract

coding assignment plagiarism datasets are a surprisingly rare occurrence
in the wild. I settled on the
, which is a C and C++ dataset with
328 authentic and 120 plagiarized assignment submission pairs.

and then compare these feature maps with a distance gated exponential

are narrowed but deepened, until only a few or a single node with many
aggregated features remains (similar to visual CNNs).

node’s neighbors and averages the result into said node.

So with Cursor Composer 2.5, we generated more data to train the model
Generate 20 task descriptions for C++ assignments, solvable in a
single source code file of around ~100-ish lines of code.
Generate 8 authentic solutions for each task, writing them
independently and without any knowledge of the other solutions.
For each authentic solution, generate 4 plagiarized solutions with
different degrees of blatancy, employing same techniques as humans
order (column-major), accumulate into local before assign
Heavy renames, casual comment, decrement loops
Lightest touch — still not copy-paste: a few renames + main
Implement a generic singly linked list template with iterator
support and use it to merge two sorted integer sequences from
the heap. Support push_back, size, forward iteration, and a free
that returns a new sorted list without mutating the inputs
Read two whitespace-separated ascending integer sequences from
stdin (sequence ends at newline; second sequence on the next
line). Output the merged sequence space-separated on one line.

Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs) can be thought of pretty similar to
difference is the aggregation function being a sum of the node’s
neighbors’ embeddings instead of a mean. The single GIN passes are
repeated in order to extend the aggregation reach to multiple hops. For
further processing, the residuals (the individual passes) are summed up
along all nodes in the graph and concatenated to form a final graph
Assuming all hidden layers also use injective activation functions, the
GIN as a whole is also injective. Put differently, every different input
graph will have a different output embedding. This makes it great for
classification tasks where we want to be able to distinguish between

High-level ML pipeline for the GIN approach
After embedding the source files into a high-dimensional vector space, we
can compute the cosine similarity between the vectors. The cosine
similarity is a measure of how similar two vectors are, and is calculated as
the dot product of the two vectors divided by the product of the
magnitudes of the two vectors, as shown in
The GIN inherent property of being injective guarantees longer
embedding vectors for bigger ASTs, which is not meaningful for
similarity of the solution approach. Through cosine similarity, we can
compare the “direction” of the encoded solutions independent of their
After training for 99250 steps, the best performing model was at 78000,
with an ideal threshold of 0.93 and an F1-Score (assuming 0.5 threshold)
on the validation set. This is significantly higher than our baseline

being able to reason about it in that space. Naturally, I performed some
dimensionality reduction on the embeddings to visualize the source file

Making this whole thing ready as web application.
With burn and Rust’s wasm32 target, we can easily compile the model
to a self contained binary executable by the browser.
weights and the model itself into a single file.
The separation between heavy embedding computation and performant
similarity calculation allows for efficient mass cross-file plagiarism
detection. This becomes a two step process:
Compute the embeddings for all source files in the dataset
Compute the similarity of every embedding with every other embedding
